Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

s## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

s## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

 ## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes

smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

 ## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

9## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a

a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

0## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

s## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

 ## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes

smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is

n## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

s## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

c## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

m## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |

o## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

t## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

 ## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

c## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

e## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

i## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a

order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

n## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

|---|---|---|

| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

 ## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes

smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

i## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.

y## Scale

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a

Perception runs through a uniform grid: one cell per `perception_radius`, and a person's neighbours are
read from the nine cells around its own. Measured with `examples/benchmark` on an M1 Max, release build,
starter pack, `tick_secs = 0.25`:

| persons | ms per society tick | amortised per 60 fps frame |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.6 | 0.04 ms (0.2%) |
| 1 000 | **13.5** | 0.9 ms (5.3%) |
| 2 000 | 49.9 | 3.1 ms (19%) |
| 5 000 | **245.1** | 15.3 ms (**92%**) |

A thousand people costs about 5% of a 60 fps budget; five thousand costs most of a frame.

**The cost is the crowd, not the search.** An earlier version scanned every pair, and the note here said
that pair count was the scale curve. It is not: measured directly, the all-pairs scan was **36 ms of a
254 ms tick** at 5 000 people. Substituting the grid is bit-identical — the same neighbours in the same
order, so the same society — and saves 3-7%.

What actually scales is **scoring**. Every `Person`-targeted activity is scored against every neighbour:
at 5 000 people on the benchmark's 40 m disc an 8 m radius holds **182** neighbours, so a tick runs
roughly `5 000 x 4 x 182 = 3.6M` consideration evaluations. The density is real, so no index removes
those. A host that needs thousands of people in contact wants fewer `Person`-targeted activities, a
smaller `perception_radius`, or a decision that samples neighbours rather than scoring them all. That is
a design question (`docs/loop/needs-decision/`), not an indexing one.
